items.title: Nicki Parrott interviewed by Monk Rowe. Utica, New York, November 6, 2010 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: when I was up here last time I worked with Dick Hyman here, and I also worked with Dick Hyman earlier in the year at Merlin’s.

ctx.x: Which I think is a big part of being a musician, especially a bass player. You’ve got to figure out what’s the situation here. How do you gain that musical knowledge? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

Um. Well it’s funny, there are different ways to lead a band, you know, and now that I’m a band leader myself a lot I’m learning how to do it and get the results and get the respect and everything, and there are some people, like when I was up here last time I worked with Dick Hyman here, and I also worked with Dick Hyman earlier in the year at Merlin’s. And someone like Dick doesn’t really want to tell you how to play but might give you a guideline, you know what I mean? Like well I think you sing that song…

That’s great advice. I’ve often felt that the bass player really is the lynchpin of the whole thing. I mean you can send the music in a direction if you want to, I mean if you want to start swinging and the rest of the band is playing in two, you can sort of like say no, we’re going this way.

items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: And that bass player, what’s her name, Parrott, Vicky is her name? ... Nicki Parrott. Wonderful

ctx.x: And I just wonder where is it going? How can it keep changing so fast? Do you have any opinions on what’s going to happen with it? When I look at this jazz party scene, it’s really wonderful to be at, I wonder how long it can keep going.
One of the most remarkable things about this party is the way that Mat [Domber] has been including women. And that bass player, what’s her name, Parrott, Vicky is her name?
